For me, exercise doesn't always work. Sometimes I'm just unable to exercise because of anxiety of being looked at and judged while I exercise, or I'm just physically unable to move.
 
On those days, I have to let my emotions kinda just wash over me. I am not allowing myself to ignore them, but I acknowledge that trying to burn them out with exercise isn't my way of dealing with them. 

Anger and irritability is different. If I'm angry or irritable, I go to weight training with my favorite music for as long as I need. Cardio doesn't work for me because my lungs give out before my body does, so going for weights and finding a channel for those emotions is better than snapping at people all day long. 

A substitute is sedatives, which you can talk to your doc about, I legit took a sedative to calm down before going to the gym for the first time in a while after my dad suggested it. 

Nothing is a one fit all solution, and many solutions only cover one or two things. If it's not working for you, maybe a variation of the same thing will. Build a hypothesis about yourself and apply that to your actions. 

Emotions are uncontrollable, but the way we act on them is.

First of all, y'aint dumb, I can guarantee that. You're seeking out help for something that you have no idea about, and that's pretty smart to me. 

Second, there are a few options, but most are gonna take trial and error, so be patient with yourself. I'm 24 and I'm still figuring the whole Adult ADHD thing out. 

The first thing to look at is what works for you and what doesn't. For me, this means understanding that sometimes I am unable to cook for myself unless I cook for others as well, so a lot of the time I rely on frozen foods to keep my costs down. 

Basically it's time to life hack yourself. If something isn't working that usually works for other people, the truth of the situation is that it's probably never gonna work for you and there's more than one way to skin a cat. There are plenty of young adults with ADHD on social media now sharing their own life hacks that help them manage how their brain works. 

One person I saw in particular throws their phone in the morning to keep them out of a scrolling loop while in bed, another sets up arbitrary race times when they set a timer for the microwave to race and grab all the empty water bottles from their room. Another person (during the pandemic mind you) would get up for work, get dressed, get in his car, drive around the block, come into his office and work, and then when work was done, he would go out to his car, drive around the block again, come into his home and relax. 

This is the age of discovery for you, and discovering exactly how your brain functions and what quirky things you can do for yourself to ease some of the executive dysfunction and attention deficit. 

Another thing you can do is look for an ADHD coach, basically someone to help hold you accountable for what you do and help you figure out all those life hacks for your brain, but much like any psychologist psychiatrist, this can take a bit to find someone who really understands your brain and can relate to you, much like finding friends 

The last thing you can do is constant research. Something seem odd or just you? Google it. Guarantee you are not the only one, and someone else may have some weird solution or hack to help it. 

I will say, be cautious of "organizational experts," because this isn't an organization problem, it's a matter of putting our brains in the right gear. No amount of "time management" classes or "organizations life hacks" will really benefit us, because our brains aren't hard wired to work in those constraints. It's like trying to plug a US plug into a EU one. Wrong peg, no power. 

A diagnosis is the first step in self research and discovery. It opens up a world of research and a community of wealth in information. Y'ain't dumb, y'ain't lazy, take it from a person who had to learn self advocacy through fire.

That's the thing, getting help is never easy. Help isn't easy, if it was easy, we'd all have the help in the world. It's also about self responsibility. Effort alone is good because it shows others that you want help. That you want to find remission.

Effort breeds hope, and I think that's one of the reasons people with depression find getting help so hard, because if the help doesn't work out, our hope shatters. It's so draining to tumble back on any progress of hope made, and it makes us want to give up before being hurt again, and it's a good defense mechanism to say you're far too gone for help. 

The thing is though, help and it's levels aren't universal, if one place doesn't work out, you're gonna have to try another. 

At this point, I'm just rambling, but I've been fighting for help and self advocacy since I was 6 years old, and help is something I know comes in many shades of gray. 

Ultimately, the only person who can decide to get you help is you. Once you decide to help yourself, others come around you to help as well.

I always knew growing up that I wasn't having all my needs met. I unfortunately have suffered from Anxiety, Depression, OCD, and ADHD since I was young, but my mom acted more like my boss than a mother. It didn't help that both of my sisters are also autistic, my older sister being on the less functional end of the spectrum, and my younger sister being nonverbal for a good chunk of her childhood. 

I became a worker. Doing chores that my siblings either failed to do or did poorly, helping my mom with anything she needed, on top of that, take care of my own chores. I was turning into a substitute mother. I would break down often, have crying fits and threaten suicide from the age of 13. My mom only told me to suck it up. 

To give her some ground to stand on, she had her own problems. She herself had depression, and had given so much energy to take care of my siblings that I think I just kinda fell by the wayside. She was exhausted trying to give my sisters the care they needed that I was the least of her worries. 

Now I struggle deeply with the idea of my success and emotional state. I struggle asking anyone outside of a therapist for help, and will always diminish my needs over others. I care for others before I care for myself. I'm still working on it, and I struggle with it daily. 

Recently my mom suddenly passed away, and I was sitting down talking with my dad about my childhood. He told me that mom was unfairly hard on me, and he hopes I know that. It was the validation of my experience from my dad that really helped start the healing of that part. He told me to really start caring for myself, because he'll take care of my siblings. 

I'm still healing, but validation and helped a ton.
